item.title: Ice Cube’s BIG3 Swaps NFTs For League Equity To Ambassador To Denmark
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Ice Cube's BIG3 exchanged Ken Howery's team-linked NFTs for league equity while pursuing a planned stock-market merger.
item.content:encoded:
Ice Cube‘s BIG3 three-on-three basketball league exchanged PayPal co-founder Ken Howery’s Fire-tier NFTs for equity under a settlement newly detailed by The Washington Sun.

Howery, who also serves as U.S. Ambassador to Denmark under the Trump administration, joined the rollout alongside Snoop Dogg.

In May 2022, the league announced that the two had teamed up to purchase all 25 Fire-tier tokens tied to the team Big3 team, Bivouac.

The report placed his NFT holdings between $100,001 and $250,000. It did not value the BIG3 HoldCo LLC units he received.

The broader buyer dispute moved into individual arbitration after purchasers accused BIG3 of “deceptive, fraudulent, and illegal marketing” over team-sale benefits. They alleged the league renamed sold teams while calling the originals “on hiatus.”

BIG3 disputed the allegations.

BIG3’s original 2022 package mixed fan access with a say in team decisions. Each franchise was allotted 25 Fire-tier tokens and 975 Gold-tier tokens, giving the offer a team-by-team structure.

Fire-tier tokens were offered at $25,000 each, compared with $5,000 for Gold-tier tokens.

Buyers were promised game access and votes on team representatives, uniform colors and league awards. Fire holders were also offered the right to use their team’s name and logo to make and sell artwork and designs.

The financial benefits came with conditions. Fire-tier holders were promised a collective 40 percent of net proceeds from a future team sale, subject to regulatory approval. Separately, the package offered an opportunity to obtain shares at the initial public offering price if BIG3 went public.

The Sun also cited an October disclosure that BIG3 had “entered into settlement agreements with two NFT purchasers” in 2025, followed by two more in the first half of 2026.

In June, BIG3 and Graf Global announced plans to merge, creating a path from holding-company equity to public stock.

The terms called for existing equity and equity-linked holdings to convert into shares of the combined company at closing.

The June agreement valued BIG3 at $290 million before new funding and potential earnouts. Its closing conditions included shareholder and regulatory approvals, a stock-exchange listing and at least $50 million in net cash proceeds. Howery’s units would become public-company stock only if the merger closes.

item.title: Anuel AA Reveals How Eminem Helped Shape His Music During Prison
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Anuel AA tells SiriusXM's Shade 45 how Eminem's 'Stan' and 'Mockingbird' inspired prison-era recordings and personal songs.
item.content:encoded:
Anuel AA says Eminem influenced some of the most personal records of his career, including a Spanish adaptation of “Stan” that connected with fans while the Puerto Rican rapper was behind bars.

Speaking with D-Stroy on SiriusXM’s Shade 45, Anuel recalled recording his version of Eminem’s 2000 hit in prison, when listeners had heard little from him since his incarceration.

“Eminem was a legend, bro. I did the ‘Stan’ hook in Spanish when I was in prison, and that’s a big-ass song in my career,” Anuel told D-Stroy. “Like, people related a lot to it.”

He explained that the recording marked an important moment because he believed it was among the first music fans heard from him after he was locked up. The track, “Me Contagié,” featuring Kendo Kaponi, drew on “Stan,” the Eminem song built around a sample of Dido’s “Thank You.”

“It was the first song I dropped, the first song, or the first, even, I think that was the first thing I said or did since I went to prison,” Anuel said. “People never heard from me again until that song came out, you feel me?”

The influence extended beyond that recording’s success. Anuel also recalled making a deeply personal song for his mother over the instrumental from Eminem’s “Mockingbird.”

He described it as a record about the hardships he faced before his career took off, including fears that eventually became real.

“I did a song for my mom with the ‘Mockingbird’ beat,” Anuel said. “It’s a song talking about my life, about the struggles before the success, you feel me?”

He said some of the events he hoped his mother would never have to witness eventually happened, including his incarceration. That made listening back to the song especially difficult.

“A lot of the bad things I said in the song that I didn’t want to happen, I didn’t want my mom to see me going through that, they happened,” he said. “And I ended up in prison.”

Anuel’s prison-era breakthrough is a significant chapter of his career. He was incarcerated following a 2016 federal firearms case and continued attracting an audience while serving his sentence.

He later released his debut album, Real Hasta la Muerte, in 2018, the year he was released.

The rapper has discussed the recording before.

During a 2024 appearance on the Spanish television program El Hormiguero, he described making his adaptation of “Stan” by telephone while incarcerated and said the song took off when he feared his music career was finished.

On Shade 45, however, he went further by describing the creative lesson he took from Eminem. Rather than limiting himself to street records, romantic tracks or diss songs, he realized he could bring family relationships into his lyrics.

“With Eminem, I learned like you don’t just do music for girls, commercials, street songs, or diss songs,” Anuel explained, “but you could do music, too, for your mom, for your daughter.”

“Eminem is a big inspiration for me in my whole career,” he added. “Really, really big, for real.”

item.title: Flo Milli Wins Dismissal Of “Never Lose Me” Copyright Lawsuit
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Flo Milli won dismissal of a copyright lawsuit targeting "Never Lose Me" after a judge rejected the plaintiff's ownership claim.
item.content:encoded:
Flo Milli has won dismissal of a copyright lawsuit targeting her breakthrough hit “Never Lose Me” and seeking at least $1 million in damages.

Billboard reports Judge Andre Birotte Jr. rejected songwriter Shamar Deal’s infringement claim after finding that Deal did not own the beat at the center of the case. That ownership issue proved decisive because a plaintiff must hold copyright rights before pursuing an infringement claim.

Deal sued in June 2025 and named Flo Milli, Babyface Ray, 42 Dugg, producer Gerreaux Katana, Sony Music Entertainment and EMPIRE Distribution as defendants. His complaint said he bought an exclusive 10-year license to Katana’s beat “Youu” through the instrumental marketplace Traktrain in 2019.

The dispute began after Katana later licensed the beat for Babyface Ray and 42 Dugg’s 2023 song “Ron Artest.” Flo Milli then sampled “Ron Artest” for “Never Lose Me,” which led Deal to argue that both tracks infringed rights he believed came with his earlier license.

That path made the case unusually layered. Deal’s theory depended on rights he said began with his deal for “Youu,” continued through the use of that beat on “Ron Artest” and then reached Flo Milli through her sample.

The judge’s ownership finding stopped the claim at its first step. Without ownership of the underlying composition, Deal could not carry an infringement case through the later recordings.

Judge Birotte found that Deal’s agreement did not make him the copyright owner. The ruling cut off his infringement theory against the artists and companies he sued, even though the complaint described the original license as exclusive.

The case put one of Flo Milli’s biggest records under a legal cloud more than a year after it changed her career.

Released in late 2023, “Never Lose Me” became her first Billboard Hot 100 entry and eventually reached the Top 20. The song’s momentum carried into a remix featuring SZA and Cardi B and helped anchor her album Fine Ho, Stay.

For Flo Milli, the decision protects the record that moved her from a fast-rising rapper into a wider pop conversation.

The Mobile, Alabama, artist had already built a strong following through projects such as Ho, Why Is You Here? and You Still Here, Ho?, but “Never Lose Me” gave her a new level of radio, streaming and chart reach.

The dismissal leaves the song’s release history intact and ends Deal’s copyright claim against Flo Milli over the sample chain connecting “Youu,” “Ron Artest” and “Never Lose Me.”

item.title: D-Block Europe And Young Adz Take First Official UK Rap Chart No. 1
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: D-Block Europe and Young Adz led the first Official UK Rap Chart with What U Wanna Do, ahead of Fakemink, Skepta and EsDeeKid.
item.content:encoded:
D-Block Europe and Young Adz claimed the first No. 1 on the Official UK Rap Chart with “What U Wanna Do,” putting the South London act at the front of a new weekly ranking for British rap.

The November 6-12 chart placed Fakemink and Skepta’s “Chiltern Firehouse” at No. 2, followed by EsDeeKid’s “Bandit” at No. 3. Morrisson took fourth with “Cos Of You” and Skepta rounded out the top five with “Pandora’s Box.”

D-Block Europe also appeared at No. 9 with French Montana on “Rich Low Life.” Another entry credited to D-Block Europe and Young Adz, “Turn Off The Light,” landed at No. 24.

The first list also included BexBlu and Paul Stephan’s “Sound Of The South” at No. 6, M Huncho’s “Anonymous” at No. 7 and Suggz, Zeddy East and Deed0t’s “Been Around” at No. 8. Nines and J Styles completed the top 10 with “Freestyle.”

The ranking combines UK sales and streams for eligible British rap singles. BBC Radio 1Xtra partnered with Official Charts for a weekly countdown hosted by Kenny Allstar during his Friday night show, which airs from 9 p.m. to 11 p.m. UK time.

The November 6 broadcast opened that partnership. The new chart gives British rap its own weekly measure alongside the wider singles and album rankings, with both established performers and emerging acts eligible to appear. Official Charts will publish each new list on Fridays.

D-Block Europe’s chart showing followed the release of Worldwide Wave, their joint album with French Montana. The September 11 project contained 19 tracks, including “RICO” and “Rich Low Life,” the latter featuring Max B.

The group had already built a record on the main album chart. DBE World reached No. 6 in 2023, giving them seven UK Top 10 albums, the most for a British rap act at that point.

On the first UK Rap Chart, “What U Wanna Do” was listed with one week on the ranking and a peak of No. 1.

item.title: Michael Jackson’s Thriller Gets A Vinyl Lift Back To No. 2
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Michael Jackson's Thriller returned to No. 2 as Halloween reissues helped lift vinyl sales to their highest tracked week.
item.content:encoded:
Michael Jackson returned to No. 2 on the Billboard 200 with Thriller, and record buyers played a big part in getting the album there.

The 1982 release sold 19,000 vinyl copies during the Halloween tracking week, according to Billboard. That is its biggest vinyl week since Luminate began tracking sales electronically in 1991.

The No. 2 finish is the album’s highest position since 1984. Jackson last reached that spot with Xscape, which debuted there in May 2014.

Vinyl accounted for about 86% of its 22,000 album sales. Across purchases, streams and track sales, Thriller earned 55,000 equivalent album units, up 89%. It rose from No. 13.

The buying surge coincided with a fresh set of physical editions. Golden Pearl vinyl, a red-and-black marble pressing and a gold metallic cassette all carried October 30 release dates, putting their arrival one day before Halloween.

The two colored records were priced at $22.98 each, while the cassette was $19.98. The Golden Pearl edition was offered as a direct-to-consumer exclusive. Each product listing limited purchases to four copies per customer.

The listed track programs run through nine songs, opening with “Wanna Be Startin’ Somethin'” and closing with “The Lady In My Life.” Buyers get the familiar album in new physical forms, including “Billie Jean,” “Beat It,” and its title track.

Jackson’s Halloween chart returns have produced milestones before.

As AllHipHop reported last year, the song “Thriller” reached the Hot 100’s Top 10 again, giving him Top 10 hits across six decades. This week, the album comes close to the summit of a different chart.

The record also entered Halloween with renewed interest built earlier in 2026. The April release of the biopic “Michael” sent Jackson’s catalog back up the charts, with Thriller returning to the Billboard 200’s Top 10.

That gave the album another major audience moment months before the seasonal rush.

Streaming still supplied the largest share of this week’s album units at 32,000. But purchases grew 335%, putting the physical catalog business at the center of this return. The results cover October 30 through November 5 and appear on the November 14 chart.

item.title: Travis Scott’s Cactus Jack Sets November 18 Heat Jersey Drop
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Travis Scott's Cactus Jack fan uniform drops at Miami's November 18 game, a day before the GTA album featuring his song "RHYNO."
item.content:encoded:
Travis Scott’s Cactus Jack is heading into the Miami Heat’s Vice City night with a Nike fan uniform set for a November 18 release at Kaseya Center. The drop gives his brand a retail date alongside his music in the Grand Theft Auto VI rollout.

The Swingman jersey carries pink “Vice City” lettering, a “VI” mark and six pink stars. The players’ version keeps the Heat name, with a reversed Nike Swoosh and Cactus Jack details. Matching shorts accompany both designs.

The fan uniform is part of a larger merchandise campaign. The surrounding Court Culture catalog lists products from several other collaborations, including a $55 Court Culture x Duvin “Vice City Pool Service” pocket tee and a $50 Court Culture x New Era “Vice City” snapback.

A Court Culture x The Wild Collective satin bomber is listed at $168. Those are separately branded pieces in the broader Vice City collection, while the Nike x Cactus Jack uniform is tied to the November 18 event. The different product names matter for fans following Scott’s contribution to the campaign.

His recording role is already in place.

“RHYNO,” produced by Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo, was among the first six singles introduced for Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album on September 17.

The album brings together 34 original tracks through a partnership with Atlantic Records, with a November 19 release alongside the game.

Its opening batch of singles also included Yung Lean’s “That’s It,” featuring Future and Metro Boomin, and music from PinkPantheress, Morgan Wallen, Rauw Alejandro and Keith Richards.

The Heat host Milwaukee on November 18, with tipoff set for 7 P.M. Eastern and a custom Vice City court planned for the night. The fan jersey will go on sale at the arena in limited quantities.

The music follows on a separate retail schedule the next day: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album is due on vinyl and CD as well as streaming services, with liquid-filled and splatter vinyl editions among the announced formats.

item.title: Gazir Sets Guinness Record With 197 Rap Battle Wins In 12 Hours
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Gazir won 197 of 200 freestyle battles in a Guinness record challenge with four extended breaks of four minutes each.
item.content:encoded:
Gazir earned a Guinness World Records title after 200 freestyle battles, completing a challenge with four four-minute rest breaks. He finished with 197 wins and three losses.

The November 7 event at Laboral Ciudad de la Cultura in Gijón, Spain, gave him the record for the most rap battles contested in 12 hours, according to EFE.

To complete the challenge, Gazir needed at least 190 wins, leaving room for 10 defeats. His final score put him seven victories above that target, with a 98.5 percent win rate across the day.

The format also explains why 200 battles meant facing 250 opponents. He had 150 one-on-one contests and another 50 against two MCs at once. Those matchups were split into 10 blocks, each containing 20 battles.

Gazir had described the appeal in a pre-event EFE interview.

“There are skills in my freestyle I don’t have time to show in four battles,” he said, translated from Spanish.

A speech therapist, singing teacher, physical trainer, nutritionist and psychologist helped him prepare for the attempt.

The basic format had MCs trading four-bar turns, with six turns per side.

Judges had to pick a winner without an extra tiebreak round, and the schedule left 20 seconds to move from one battle to the next.

The longer breaks came after every 40 battles: four four-minute pauses. Hosts, DJs and judges rotated during those stops, while Gazir remained the only competitor required to complete the full run.

Babi, Skone and Bnet accounted for his three defeats.

“My job is to ensure each battle is legal,” the Guinness adjudicator told EFE during the event, translated from Spanish.

The audience helped choose the last obstacle.

Voting opened October 21 to select Gazir’s final opponent, and fans picked Mexican MC Aczino, whose three international Red Bull Batalla championships came in 2017, 2021 and 2022.

That last title had come at Gazir’s expense in the 2022 international final in Mexico City. Four years later, Aczino faced him in battle 200, in a lineup that placed a national champion or international podium finisher at the end of each block.

item.title: Bradford Cohen Calls For Lil Durk’s Release After AllHipHop Contraband Report
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Bradford Cohen urged Lil Durk's release and criticized prosecutors' contraband argument after sharing AllHipHop's reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Bradford Cohen called for Lil Durk to be released on bond after sharing AllHipHop’s report on the federal contraband investigation prosecutors cited in their fight to keep the rapper jailed.

The criminal-defense attorney used his @lawronin Instagram account to criticize the government’s reliance on alleged jail-rule violations, arguing that the claims were a familiar way to oppose release when the underlying case was weak.

“This is one of the oldest plays in the game. When your argument is weak say the Defendant cant even follow instructions in the prison,” Cohen wrote.

His post displayed AllHipHop’s November 4 story, “Lil Durk Faces Contraband Investigation As Feds Fight His Release.”

That report detailed prosecutors’ allegations that Durk used unauthorized communication devices and helped bring contraband into the Metropolitan Detention Center in Los Angeles.

Prosecutors argued that his conduct in custody showed he would not follow restrictions outside jail. They accused him of making hundreds of unauthorized calls, using other inmates’ phone access and refusing a cell search.

Cohen rejected the government’s framing.

“Makes the government look petty in this case as they were already losers,” he wrote.

The reference followed Durk’s September 11 acquittal on all five charges tried in the murder-for-hire prosecution arising from the 2022 Los Angeles shooting that killed Saviay’a “Lul Pab” Robinson. Prosecutors had accused Durk of financing an attack targeting Robinson’s cousin, Quando Rondo.

Lil Durk remained detained on separate murder-in-aid-of-racketeering and firearm charges, including allegations tied to Stephon Mack’s January 2022 killing in Chicago. He pleaded not guilty, and the remaining trial was set for August 30, 2027.

Cohen’s criticism went beyond the contraband claims. He argued that prosecutors applied their public-safety concerns differently when defendants agreed to cooperate and described pretrial detention as pressure to strike a deal.

“Bond is for the most part used as leverage. Leverage to flip and leverage to plea,” Cohen wrote.

Durk’s lawyers offered future music royalties, publishing income and earnings from his name, image and likeness as security for his release. The proposal also included property and assets pledged by supporters, with Sony backing a guarantee capped at $1 million.

Jay-Z submitted a letter supporting release, while J. Cole and former Cook County State’s Attorney Kim Foxx also backed the request. Robinson’s family said it did not object if the court considered bond appropriate.

Judge Michael W. Fitzgerald heard arguments on November 4 and took the request under submission without immediately ruling. The prosecution opposed release based on its assessment of flight risk, public safety and the alleged conduct in custody.

Cohen backed the defense proposal and urged the judge to approve it.

“The judge should GRANT him a bond. This is a very strong bond package. If he does, this will be another ding in the governments case. They need to just cut bait,” he wrote.

item.title: Adrien Broner Reportedly Okay, DeenTheGreat Weighs Going Solo
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Adrien Broner's stream partner DeenTheGreat weighed a solo path as he questioned claims about a bag after the concert scare.
item.content:encoded:
Adrien Broner is doing okay and managed to avoid a hospital stay after a crazy video showed him passed out in a wheelchair.

The former four-division boxing champ needed help during a night out on Saturday, November 7.

He was at Skilla Baby’s “The Price of Fame Tour” stop at The Belasco in Los Angeles.

As the night played out on a Kick stream, medics tended to Broner and others helped him down a flight of stairs.

He was placed in a wheelchair and taken out of the venue.

In related news, Blueface denied rumors his crew stole Broner’s bag, supposedly holding $50,000 to $100,000, on his Sunday stream, TMZ reported.

DeenTheGreat, Broner’s stream partner, asked if there was any cash in the bag.

He spoke in a video posted on his own channel Sunday, as he went through clips and claims about the night.

“I don’t know if he had bread in that, though,” Deen said.

He warned that short clips could leave out key parts of a night. He also said the bag could have been returned and then lost.

Deen spoke about the strain on their work together. He said Broner had to want to change and suggested working with other people if that did not happen.

While he pushed back at taking blame for Broner’s choices, he credited their on-screen chemistry with drawing in fans.

Their work had already moved beyond streams.

On October 15, Broner joined Deen and producer Hitmaka on “Purple App Killa,” a song aimed at Kai Cenat. The official upload listed both men as collaborators. They appeared in its video after sharing clips of work on the song.

In that Sunday upload, Deen said Broner was missing a key week for them, with New York radio shows ahead.

He linked that concern to what he saw as a lack of commitment from Broner. He said fans had seen how much he had tried to help.

That was why he raised the chance of going solo. Deen said it was hard to keep working with Broner, but left room for the two to link up from time to time.

“I love you as a brother, business partner, whatever, bro,” he said.

item.title: MC Lyte’s VH1 Jacket Enters Rock Hall Exhibit
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: MC Lyte's 2006 VH1 Hip Hop Honors jacket joins the Rock Hall exhibit, with free local access offered on November 22.
item.content:encoded:
MC Lyte‘s jacket from the 2006 VH1 Hip Hop Honors is among the pieces in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame’s new inductee exhibit, bringing a career tribute into the museum.

Axios Cleveland identified the jacket as one of the artifacts. The museum set November 9 as the exhibition’s official opening, after a members-only preview on November 6. The show represents all 18 members of its 2026 induction class.

The jacket reaches back to a night when younger women in rap performed Lyte’s music in her honor.

At the 2006 ceremony at New York’s Hammerstein Ballroom, Lil’ Kim, Remy Ma and Da Brat covered “Lyte as a Rock.” Lyte was an honoree alongside artists including Rakim, Beastie Boys and Wu-Tang Clan.

AllHipHop covered that tribute at the time. It put Lyte’s records in the hands of another generation of rappers, with her own performance part of the show; 20 years later, an item from that evening is part of another institution’s account of her career.

Her recording milestones include the 1988 debut Lyte as a Rock, followed by Eyes on This in 1989 and the Grammy-nominated “Ruffneck.”

Those records established a catalog she has continued to bring to live audiences while working as an actress, DJ and entrepreneur.

The current celebration also runs through her Road To The Hall Of Fame tour. Its Atlanta bookings at City Winery fall on November 9 and 10, with both shows listed for 8 P.M. Eastern time. The venue lists both nights as sold out and offers a waitlist.

In AllHipHop’s September tour interview, Lyte outlined roughly 90-minute shows with stories and conversation alongside her catalog.

She planned to carry those sets without depending on guest appearances. Her September studio update also put her back to work with producer Warryn Campbell.

The Rock Hall ceremony is set for November 14 at Los Angeles’ Peacock Theater.

In Cleveland, Cuyahoga County residents can visit the museum free with an RSVP on November 22, from 10 A.M. to 5 P.M. That community day includes the new exhibit, select “Soul Train” footage and performances by artist-in-residence alumni.
